And then I see a small businessman tearing his hair out because he has to have 60 Windows machines to run his business, but Microsoft keeps telling him that most of his 60 licenses are not valid. The small businessman bought from reputable vendors, but either some of those vendors were lying or else Microsoft is lying about the licenses being invalid. Regardless of who is lying, this is Microsoft setting up an economic moat.

Microsoft really does push garbage products. Even if you are an MCSE and you go through all recommended maintenance procedures, you still get blue screens of death on older models and various crashes on newer models. Microsoft is mostly to blame for encouraging people to use its products, but IMHO businessmen should accept some responsibility: if they had the foresight to support Microsoft competitors such as Linux, they would not be locked into a situation where Microsoft products are unavoidable.

Microsoft is bad for everybody. This means that almost every computer company can lower its quality standards and still smirkingly defend their products as "more reliable than Microsoft."

Microsoft's default awfulness has become so standard that no one hanged when Microsoft's shoddy products endangered lives:

The Yorktown last September suffered a systems failure when bad data was fed into its computers during maneuvers off the coast of Cape Charles, Va.

The ship had to be towed into the Naval base at Norfolk, Va., because a database overflow caused its propulsion system to fail, according to Anthony DiGiorgio, a civilian engineer with the Atlantic Fleet Technical Support Center in Norfolk.

Because Microsoft systems fail so often, Microsoft had to adopt Linux for mission-critical machines and now hopes to extend its tentacles into the Linux world.

Microsoft was able to establish its near-monopoly because free markets worked well enough. But the more that Microsoft enforces its monopoly, the more ordinary businessmen suffer. Even if I could set up a perfectly fair economy, some people would have natural talent and would probably establish monopoly positions. Some of those monopolies would survive until smacked down by anti-trust action.

It seems that free markets can arise anywhere that humans can survive. But perhaps it is not enough for free markets to arise; perhaps free markets must be able to survive the tyranny of monopolists. I doubt that top-down regulation will help, because top-down regulators have punished Microsoft for illegal monopolistic practices and still Microsoft is pushing shoddy garbage on (mostly) helpless consumers.

How did Microsoft get its foothold? One factor was that Bill Gates was born into wealth and privilege and had a very good social support network. Then IBM made a crucial mistake. IBM had previously maintained a huge and complicated supply network with a great deal of redundancy. In most cases, IBM had at least two potential suppliers for any component. However, IBM failed to support multiple operating systems for its PC platform in 1981; rather than supporting both Digital Research's CP/M and Microsoft's ripoff version of CP/M, IBM allowed Microsoft's ripoff version to become standard, in part because:

IBM marketed both CP/M and PC DOS for US$240 and US$40, respectively, with PC DOS eventually becoming the standard because of its lower price.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Microsoft#1975%E2%80%931985:_The_founding_of_Microsoft

Part of a possible solution for protecting free markets is to always be on the lookout for potential Microsoft situations and to use social force (preferably bottom-up social pressure, not top-down regulation) to prevent any new Microsoft from arising.
